items.originalTitle: ‘A savagely brutal map’: Senate GOP braces for 2028
items.author: Meredith Lee Hill
items.title: ‘A savagely brutal map’: Senate GOP braces for 2028
items.summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno isn’t sugarcoating things. The incoming chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee will be in charge of defending 19 GOP seats in 2028 — and he’ll need to flip at least six more to regain control of the Senate majority. “Looking at it right now, it's absolutely a savagely brutal map,” the Ohio Republican said in an interview on Capitol Hill. After a historic midterms shellacking, Moreno is in the hot seat as he looks to navigate his chamber — and the party — through a rebuilding of its brand and its base over next two years. Republicans will likely have just 44 seats heading into 2028. They need to hold onto seats in battleground states like Wisconsin and North Carolina, while trying to flip seats held by Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly in Arizona, John Fetterman in Pennsylvania, Raphael Warnock in Georgia and Catherine Cortez Masto in Nevada. Moreno and his team have interviewed a handful of candidates over the last few days to be the next NRSC executive director, according to four people with direct knowledge of the matter, granted anonymity to discuss private conversations. Republicans expect Chris Grant, a former Moreno and Trump campaign staffer who now runs his own firm, to serve as a main outside GOP consultant for the committee. On top of the grueling map ahead, the Ohio Republican is facing the additional task of working with a lame duck president who still wields immense power over the GOP and its primaries. Then there’s the vice president, who is likely to run for president himself in the same two-year sprint. Moreno is close with both of those men. Asked how involved he expects the White House to be in GOP primaries and recruiting going forward, he replied, “We’re going to work on all of that.” It’ll be a complicated path forward. Moreno, over the past cycle has been unwilling to cast blame on President Donald Trump or Vice President JD Vance. Days before the midterm elections, he said if Republicans lost, it would be because people were “pissed off” about high gas prices. He’s unlikely to completely distance himself and the NRSC brand from the president's influence. But the party is currently undergoing a reckoning of how closely to align with the president after voters delivered an uncompromising rebuke of Trump’s economic agenda. Across the country, several battlegrounds and once-thought-to-be-safe red territory fell to Democratic hands. Trump in the 2026 cycle angered many Senate Republicans by supporting a primary challenge against Sen. John Cornyn of Texas — a move they privately say cost them north of $200 million as they tried, in vain, to save Ken Paxton’s imperiled campaign. The president also supported a primary challenge against Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, and pushed Sen. Thom Tillis to decide to retire in highly competitive North Carolina. One of the biggest challenges before Moreno and Senate Republicans after the midterms wipeout is to find candidates who can win a general election in highly competitive states, while also making it through GOP primaries where Trump will be a major factor. They’ll need to push back on the White House if the president tries, once again, to intervene — though that’s easier said than done. “There will be no patience for bad recruits this cycle,” said one senior Republican granted anonymity to discuss internal conversations, referring to the implosions of Paxton, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and other Republicans who were hand-picked by Trump. The White House referred POLITICO to Trump's post-midterms comments, where he blamed his party’s losses on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot and said he brought several candidates "closer to victory," though they ultimately lost. Senate Majority Leader John Thune — who will be the minority leader next year — and his team plan to be heavily involved in recruitment efforts, according to two people involved in the conversations, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Their goal, one of the people said, is “to make sure we have our strongest possible candidates on the ballot in 2028.” Moreno is already trying to find a GOP recruit in his home state of Ohio to run against incoming Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, whose term will be up again in 2028 after he won a special election against GOP Sen. Jon Husted earlier this month. The new NRSC chair said he’s looking for “somebody who can beat the crap out of Sherrod Brown.” Husted in private conversations hasn’t completely ruled out another bid, but he’s indicated he’s unlikely to run again, according to three people with knowledge of the matter, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Ohio Republicans expect former state Sen. Kevin Coughlin to explore a potential Senate bid. And they’re watching Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio), who just lost his reelection. Husted did not respond to a request for comment. A Turner spokesperson said in a statement that the representative "has been approached by several people about this and is keeping all his options open.” If Vance doesn’t seek his own presidential bid, Republicans in his home state are holding a long-shot hope that he, too, might consider a return to his old job. “JD Vance would be a dream candidate,” said one Ohio Republican. items.originalTitle: Poll: Most Americans think a Democrat will be the next president
items.author: Jason Beeferman
items.title: Poll: Most Americans think a Democrat will be the next president
items.summary: Nearly twice as many Americans expect a Democrat to win the presidency in 2028 than they do a Republican, a new POLITICO Poll finds . Even one in five of President Donald Trump’s own 2024 voters believe Republicans will lose the White House, a bad sign for the GOP as it struggles to recover from widespread losses this cycle and figure out its identity after spending a decade orbiting around Trump. Just 60% of Trump voters believe Republicans will keep the White House. Democratic voters are far more confident about their own party, according to the survey conducted by PF Global in the days after the midterm: Among voters who backed Kamala Harris, 87% expect Democrats to win in 2028. Beneath the unity is disagreement over what kind of nominee to pick. Pluralities of voters agree the next president should be a fighter when asked to choose from a list of qualities. But voters across the ideological spectrum also said they want other things from the country’s 48th president. While 43% of Harris voters want “a fighter,” 40% also selected “a progressive” and 34% chose “creative.” Among Trump voters, the 45% said they want to see “a conservative” elected president, surpassing the 39% who picked “a fighter.” They're also divided over what background their nominees should come from. Nearly three in 10 Trump voters say they would prefer the next president be someone who has not worked in Trump’s administration. That number rises to 46% among Trump voters who don’t identify as MAGA, whereas 82% of his loyal MAGA base would prefer the next president be someone who did work for Trump. That debate is playing out in real-time among top GOP leaders and lawmakers. More and more Hill Republicans are eyeing Secretary of State Marco Rubio for 2028, who they say is less associated with the midterm bloodbath than Vice President JD Vance. Others say the nominee should be someone entirely outside of Trump’s direct orbit. “As much as I like Rubio, and as much as I like Vance, they can't be our nominee,” said Dan McMaster, the chair of Michigan’s Shiawassee County Republican Party. “We need to get a Republican as far away from Trump as possible, and even then, I think it's going to be a battle.” “You've got to have some fresh blood in there, and you've got to have someone that has some distance from the crap that's gone on the last two years,” said one GOP strategist who worked on multiple House races last cycle and was granted anonymity to speak candidly about their own party. In a statement, Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said the president isn’t going anywhere. "President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party who's cut taxes, lowered drug costs, and secured our border,” Baldassarre said. “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our base and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win in 2028." The White House also pointed POLITICO to separate polling earlier this month that shows Trump’s approval rating sits at 75% with all Republicans and jumps to 93% with those who identify as MAGA. “President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson. On election night earlier this month, Trump blamed his party’s losses on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot, telling POLITICO by phone , “I wasn't on the ballot. If I was on the ballot, we would have won; we would have won it all very easily.” Meanwhile, Democrats have their own disagreements to figure out as they select their nominee. This cycle’s blue wave has bolstered the progressive wing of the party, which has long hoped to prove their candidates can win in purple battlegrounds, not just in safe-blue states. But the poll reveals skepticism remains — at least among moderates — over whether progressive wins in 2026 can translate to the presidential stage in 2028. The survey found a majority of progressive Democrats — 63% — want a progressive to be president, compared with just 23% of moderates who say the same. Half of progressive Democrats are convinced that being a progressive is a quality that will get their candidate elected in 2028. Moderates are less certain of that, though they’re also not as confident in their own faction: Just 37% think being a moderate is a quality that ensures the Democratic candidate wins. “Whoever's running for president has seen what's happened and also has seen the power of our movement, and so this is something that could be carried on to 2028,” said progressive New Jersey Democratic Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, reflecting on the wins he and others enjoyed this cycle. “Despite it being the most expensive elections in history, we showed that people are able to beat out money when we come together.” And with Democrats winning Senate seats in deep-red states like Kansas and Mississippi for the first time in decades, many now argue that the entire map is in play for 2028. The poll found that 60% of Democrats think the party should focus their efforts on winning all states in the presidential election, even ones that seemed like deep Republican areas, rather than focus on holding the states where they know their supporters are. Republicans felt the same, with 56% also arguing for an “all states” approach as the party races to rebuild in territory they once thought was safe. “I have been very, very loud about the fact that the path to the presidency leads through the South,” said Democratic strategist Dallas Jones, who ran statewide Black voter engagement for Lone Star Rising PAC, the outside group that supported Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico. “But again, we don't make investments there. We're playing the same electoral map with the same swing states.”

items.originalTitle: How The Verge is picking which Black Friday deals to share
items.author: Cameron Faulkner
items.title: How The Verge is picking which Black Friday deals to share
items.summary: For the past month, we’ve been inundated with Black Friday deals, signaling what’s to come on the biggest shopping day of the year in the US. We routinely get dozens of press releases a day, coming from brands big and small that hope that we’ll publicize these offers. Of course, the companies would prefer that we don’t do any research on these deals to see if they’re actually good, and most don’t provide any of the necessary context we’re looking for when vetting them. Most indicators of a good deal are confusing — not just for us, but for anyone who’s shopping. Groundwork Collaborative recently published its findings about the unclear manner in which Amazon displays deals. Its researchers tracked a selection of products ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025, and they claim that nearly one in three products advertised as deals on Amazon didn’t offer savings during the actual shopping events. The investigation also found that nearly a tenth of the deals it examined were more expensive during the sales events than on some days in the month leading up to them. Something we commonly see on Amazon and attempt to correct for in our coverage are good deals with inflated discount claims. As in, the original retail amount (the “list” price) is sometimes higher than the usual day-to-day price to make the savings seem more substantial. Sometimes, the manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP) is what’s shown, though that’s not always the case. In a recent statement to investigative journalist Ronan Farrow , an unattributed Amazon spokesperson shared that its “List Price” can also be aggregated from the past 90 to 180 days of prices, not the past 30 days as Groundwork Collaborative’s research states, and is based on prices from Amazon itself and other competing retailers. However, in our experience, the confusing way pricing and discounts are communicated isn’t limited to Amazon. View this post on Instagram The group’s findings show how easy it is to distrust the prices you see, especially online, where dynamic pricing sometimes comes into play. Regardless of retailer practices, we understand the importance of curating what you see on The Verge with care. Vetting deals for coverage consideration is a big, albeit invisible, part of our jobs, even outside of big shopping events. Most of what we’re pitched day to day, or what we see in our respective feeds, never hits the site because it doesn’t meet our standards. Even when the deal is for a product we’ve tested and really enjoy — our north star for what to cover on the deals front — that alone doesn’t guarantee coverage. We often skip covering deals that aren’t as good as a retailer or brand made them seem. Or maybe the deal is good, but it returns every week, lasts only a few hours, or it’s available only with a premium membership. Alternatively, the deal might only be available from a retailer none of us has heard of or shopped at. Needless to say, we consider a ton of factors. With Black Friday coming up, you deserve transparency from us so you know — whether it’s this month or a random day in February — that you’re looking at an actual deal when you visit our site. The most basic criteria we use to judge whether a deal is good is whether we like the product enough to write about it and whether its price has dropped. Then we assess whether the discount is actually worth your attention. That part of the conversation has become a little complicated in the past year. RAMageddon and the ripple effects of higher tariffs have, in some cases, substantially impacted pricing and, by extension, the deals we cover. We follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass For products hit by recent price hikes, the new deal prices sometimes amount to the original sticker price, or close to it. Several of us would nod our heads with you if you think, “Hey, that’s not a deal; that’s just the original price. I’m no fool!” But it’s also technically a deal for many of us who are just trying to save wherever possible. Along those lines, we’ll sometimes highlight ways to save on digital or physical goods by buying discounted gift cards, which can be used to buy in-demand products. These methods are the only way to get any kind of deal on Grand Theft Auto VI before launch, for example. To help us stay aware of price drops, we also use free tracking tools like CamelCamelCamel and Keepa, which provide an independent read on Amazon’s historical pricing. ( You can use them, too! ) They’ll alert us when a product we like — and that we know you’ll probably like — goes on sale. Amazon also has its own Alexa for Shopping tool , which can show up to a year of pricing data and perform several other AI chatbot-like actions, including automatically buying products on your behalf. In my experience, Amazon’s historical pricing data usually aligns with non-Amazon-affiliated companies. However, none of them are perfect. Even the third-party tools we use don’t always display the record-low prices we’ve covered, for whatever reason. All of this to say, there are a lot of ins and outs, but we follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass. We cast a fairly large net for products across a range of categories ahead of the holidays, including some that don’t often get much play on The Verge . However, of the thousands of deals that we’ve seen ahead of Black Friday, you’re seeing the mere dozens of standouts that we’ve tested or used in our personal lives within each category — headphones, TVs, gaming accessories, smart home tech, etc. — that meet our criteria for being good products at noteworthy prices.

items.originalTitle: Billie Jean King Had Seen Other Sports Documentaries. She Wanted Hers to Be Different
items.author: Sean Gregory
items.title: Billie Jean King Had Seen Other Sports Documentaries. She Wanted Hers to Be Different
items.summary: —Courtesy of ESPN Films How did Arnold Palmer order an Arnold Palmer? You know, the half-lemonade, half-iced-tea concoction named in his honor? Steve Politi, sports columnist at NJ.com, unearthed the answer years ago , at Augusta National Golf Club, where a waitress who served Palmer his drink told him: "He leaned over and said, 'I'll have a Mr. Palmer.' Then he winked.” Along the same lines, during the U.S. Open, how does Billie Jean King tell a driver that she’s going to her own complex: the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in Flushing, N.Y., where this year more than 1.2 million fans, a new record, attended the final Grand Slam tennis tournament of the season? “Bring me to Ms. King’s,” perhaps? “No, I never do that,” says iconic tennis Hall of Famer and activist, 82, who is the subject of a new ESPN documentary, Give Me the Ball!, out on Nov. 22. Though “when they get me out there, they kind of start going, ‘Is this yours?’” So few humans experience the feeling of walking into a sprawling sports facility named in their honor. So what’s that like for King? “I never get used to it,” she says. “It's weird. To see your own name up there, I'm like, squeeze me.” In early November, King joined TIME via video to talk about why Give Me the Ball! gets real, the nature of progress for women’s sports, her glasses collection, and why she’s not done fighting for equality. (This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity) You’ve been featured in prior films, wrote a best-selling memoir, All In, and were the subject of a biopic, Battle of the Sexes, starring Emma Stone as you . What will viewers learn about you in Give Me the Ball! that they don’t already know? A lot. Personally, I don’t think most people really understand how we got the [women’s tennis] tour started. I don’t expect people to know. They’ve got their own lives. This slows things down, and they really do get a sense of what I went through trying to change things, develop things, trying to always be the first. And then the sexuality part. I had an eating disorder. I talk about that, which I think is important for people to hear because I think a lot of people have eating disorders plus other things. I think sometimes people are afraid to go to therapy. And I told [the filmmakers] how great it’s been for me. Can you recall a moment when the women’s tour got going in the early 1970s that maybe wasn’t much fun at the time, but you look back now and think, “I can’t believe how far we’ve come”? I wanted the men and women to be together. The men just turned me down all the time. They started their own ATP [Association of Tennis Professionals] in '72, so I knew we had to go on our own. We tried to convince the women. The women showed up. Everybody voted for it. We elected officers. During that meeting, I said five continents have to be represented on the board, and that really helped because a lot of the non-Americans thought it was just an American thing. And I kept saying, “No, no, it's a world vision. It's a global vision.” And I don't think they believed me until that moment. There were about 60 of us, and I can remember everybody relaxing. The non-Americans, you could just see them exhale. And I thought, “OK, this is good.” What was at stake in the Battle of the Sexes, your iconic 1973 match against Bobby Riggs ? It was about changing the hearts and minds of people. We got 90 million people to watch. The Super Bowl had 53 million that year. Women got self-confidence. Most of them came up to me and said, “I didn’t believe I had a life, and after you beat him, that changed everything.” Men, on the other hand, were very reflective. When I met President Obama, he said to me, “You know, I was 12 years old when I saw your match. And I've got two girls now. It's really helped me raise them.” Billie Jean King waves to crowds at the Astrodome in Houston as four men carry her on a throne for her match with Bobby Riggs on Sept. 20, 1973. —Associated Press You talk about your eating disorder in the film, and how it helped you medicate while coming to terms with your sexual identity. How did binging help you? Like an alcoholic, it helps numb you, and then you can just let go and go to sleep. I'm not bulimic, so I don't throw up. It helps me just totally get numb and go to sleep and not feel anything. In 1972, Ms. magazine published a “We Have Had Abortions" petition for reproductive freedom: your ex-husband, Larry King , signed your name to it without your knowledge. What did you learn from that whole experience? Talked to my mom. I knew she'd have trouble because—oh my God, she doesn't understand. Anyway, [my parents] were great, though. They went when I talked to the media. They were there. They're very loyal. Even though they're homophobic. Working through that took a long time, and Renfrew [Center for Eating Disorders] really helped. I was there for six weeks. I lived there, and I had a therapist, and I had three sessions a week. And then you have couples twice a week. You have family once a week. You're in therapy all the time. But it makes you think and feel. It’s just not fun. It’s not easy. But boy, coming out the other side is fantastic. You also discuss your ordeal with Marilyn Barnett, with whom you had an affair while married in the 1970s. Her 1981 lawsuit publicly outed you. Was it difficult reliving that era? Very. Those very painful times. And I’m living through it again with this doc. But it’s necessary. I didn’t want it to be all pabulum and goody two-shoes. Nobody has that easy a life. So the way a lot of these athletes and others do [documentaries], they’re acting like it’s just la-di-da la-di-da, boom, boom. “The tough part is being a jock and working out hard and injuries.” And I’m like, “Oh, come on.” That is a lot of it, but that’s not your whole life. I’m not going to bring up names, but when you see their docs I’m like, “Uh-huh, and?” I didn’t want that to happen with mine. How has your friendship with Elton John helped you through various challenges? We could talk about our feelings to each other. I couldn’t talk to very many people in those days. He was one of the good ones. He and I could talk about drugs, sexuality. Food was my drug. We knew that the world wouldn’t hear everything we had to say. We could keep things private. We just hit it off when we first met. It was pretty funny. We just sat for hours talking and listening to music. He's hysterical. The WNBA played Game 6 of its finals, between the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries, at 12:30 p.m. E.T. on a Thursday, as the Atlanta Hawks, the primary tenant of State Farm Arena, had a game scheduled that evening. What did you make of that? It was great they could get an arena that allowed more people to come and watch because they were getting the crowds. That was major. Was it convenient? No. Was it harder? Yes. But it’s not a perfect world. And women’s sports is still very young. Give Me the Ball! gives us a glimpse of your everyday life, like when you chose, among a suitcase full of glasses, which color to wear to match an outfit. Do you take that everywhere with you? Yes. It holds 16 glasses. People go, “Oh, did you get those from Elton?” I go, “No.” I looked at his stuff. He’s got thousands. He goes overboard a lot. I go a little bit. But not like him. He’s got a lot more money. What role do you think you played in the ascendance of women’s sports? I’m not finished. Girls are taught not to ask for what they want and need. That’s one of the things I want sports to help change. Ilana [Kloss, King’s wife] and I are really good at relationships. Relationships are everything. If you ever need to get to anybody, just tell us. We want to make a bigger, better impact and help generations that are going to follow. I’m still going full blast. items.originalTitle: How Voting Rights Impacted the 2026 Midterms
items.author: Kevin T. Morris
items.title: How Voting Rights Impacted the 2026 Midterms
items.summary: A voter fills out his ballot on Election Day, November 03, 2026 in Jackson, Mississippi. —Azariah Wells—Jackson State University/Getty Images On January 3, Scott Colom will be sworn in as the 52 nd United States Senator from Mississippi. Perhaps more importantly, Colom will be the first Black Mississippian elected to statewide office since Reconstruction —and the first Black Mississippian ever popularly elected to the U.S. Senate by voters in the Magnolia State. Black Mississippians’ outrage at the Supreme Court’s gutting of the 1965 Voting Rights Act helped put him there. That fact should inspire quick and committed congressional action to restore the law’s protections—not some misplaced hope that they are no longer needed. Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court seemingly completed its decade-long assault on the crown jewel of the Civil Rights Movement. The Voting Rights Act was passed after the 15 th Amendment’s prohibitions on race discrimination in voting had languished for nearly a full century. During that period, the State of Mississippi was often a leader in Jim Crow and white supremacist policies keeping African Americans from participating in the electoral process. Fewer than 10% of Black Mississippians were registered to vote in 1964, on the eve of the Voting Rights Act’s passage. After just four short years of federal enforcement, that number jumped to nearly 60% . At the local level, many Black Mississippians were elected for the first time. Perhaps in no other state was the Voting Rights Act more effective at helping counter race discrimination in voting. And yet, in a series of decisions stretching back to 2013’s Shelby County v. Holder , the Supreme Court has steadily eroded the Voting Rights Act. In April this year, in Louisiana v. Callais , the strategy effectively brought an end to Section 2, the law’s last remaining safeguard against discriminatory voting rules and district maps. Writing for the dissent, Justice Elena Kagan lamented the majority’s “now-completed demolition of the Voting Rights Act.” Black voters took this danger to heart; by all accounts, they turned out at extraordinarily high rates this fall, as they did in primary elections this year. But a focus on high turnout by Black voters in general obscures a more telling story. My early analysis with Arlyss Herzig at the Brennan Center indicates that turnout by Black and minority voters did not surge equally across the nation. Instead, the surge was especially pronounced in jurisdictions that, until 2013, were covered under the Voting Rights Act’s preclearance protections. In 2013, the Supreme Court in Shelby County struck down the formula determining which jurisdictions were covered, effectively ending preclearance. Those jurisdictions had to prove to the federal government that any changes to voting laws and rules wouldn’t make voters of color worse off, relative to white voters. It was in these counties that state officials have worked the hardest to dismantle those protections, and where the absence of what remained of the Voting Rights Act is felt the most acutely. Small surprise, then, that these were the counties where minority turnout spiked the most this year, even after accounting for differences among Black, Latino, and other minority voters. If the death of the Voting Rights Act was galvanizing minority voters, this is exactly what we would expect to see. In a race decided by around 5,000 votes out of nearly a million cast, it is very possible that this backlash surge could have helped put Colom over the finish line in Mississippi. But the fact that Black voters in Mississippi were able to elect the candidate they preferred should not be taken to mean that the Voting Rights Act is no longer necessary. Quite the opposite. A dramatic show of political force was needed to overcome the barriers created by the Court’s attacks on the Voting Rights Act. In fact, in Louisiana, across the Mississippi River from where Colom made history, we just saw how strong some of these structural barriers can be. Thanks to successful litigation brought under the Voting Rights Act, Black Louisianans had the ability to elect two of the state’s six members of Congress in 2024, roughly in line with their share of the population. But following the Court’s decision in Callais , lawmakers reverted to a previous map that limited Black voters’ ability to elect their preferred candidate to just one congressional district. My analysis suggests that turnout surged among Black voters who previously could, but no longer can, elect a representative of their choosing. Their turnout increased by four points this year, while the turnout of white voters in that region dropped . And yet, my research indicates that white voters—not Black voters—will be represented in Congress next year by the candidate they voted for. A similar post- Callais district map in Tennessee stripped Black voters in Nashville of their congressional representation, too. Even in Mississippi, Black voters, who make up 36% of the electorate, will be underrepresented in the House next year, with just one Black-majority district out of the state’s four. The takeaways here are clear. Scott Colom is headed to the U.S. Senate in part because Black voters are rightfully enraged by the dismantling of the Voting Rights Act. But the gutting of protections still harms minority voters around the nation; hundreds∫ of thousands of Black Louisianans and Tennesseans will now be without a preferred representative in the U.S. House because of the Supreme Court’s decision this year. The next Congress should listen to what voters are demanding: a new Voting Rights Act as bold as the one that arose out of the Civil Rights Movement, one that blocks discriminatory policies before they can take effect in elections, and that's strong enough to strike down those already on the books. The dramatic outcry at the polls has made that possible today, if only our leaders have the courage to act.

items.summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola ousted GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska — the first time in 18 years a Democrat has won a Senate race in the state. Her win gives Democrats a 56-44 edge in the Senate. Peltola was one of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s top recruits for the cycle. She overpowered a Republican rescue mission for Sullivan and allegations of misconduct against her from former staffers to flip a state President Donald Trump won by 13 points in 2024. Her victory continues the blue wave born from voters’ frustrations at high costs and the Trump administration. Peltola will return to Washington, where she will become the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate after previously holding the same distinction in the House. Her campaign had projected confidence about her path to victory as the vote count dragged on in a far-flung, rural state with long grace periods for late-arriving ballots. But her win was not without tumult. Trump’s Department of Justice sued to try to stop the certification if Sullivan lost, claiming voters could be confused by his same-name challenger. The president went so far as to call for votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan and another longshot candidate in the four-way, all-party contest to be transferred to the incumbent. The Justice Department also started probing efforts to recruit Dan J. Sullivan after a New York Times report suggesting members of Peltola’s campaign and Senate Democrats’ campaign arm were involved. Both had previously denied involvement.

items.originalTitle: America's Top Manufacturers of 2027
items.author: Olivia B. Waxman
items.title: America's Top Manufacturers of 2027
items.summary: —Illustration by TIME; Filo—Getty Images As major U.S. manufacturers have increasingly moved their production overseas in the last few decades to reduce costs, President Trump ’s hallmark global tariffs were designed to force these companies to do their manufacturing stateside. But the tariffs proved unpopular , with the conservative think tank Cato Institute reporting in August that there is no factory building boom and that manufacturing is only expanding in industries facing the lowest tariffs , like electronics. The cost of living soared so high that Democrats won control of the House and the Senate in the 2026 midterm elections on Nov. 3—though it remains to be seen to what extent they will be able to challenge President Trump’s tariffs. Despite all this, manufacturing is still one of the largest sectors of the U.S. economy, with 12.6 million manufacturing workers as of September 2026. TIME has partnered with data firm Statista to rank the companies that are thriving. The list features companies with at least $100 million in 2025 revenue and production facilities in the U.S., and analyzes company disclosures, public databases, and patent analytics. Companies were assessed on revenue growth from 2023 to 2025, as well as R&D expenditure in that same time frame; and workforce growth, retention, and workplace safety through data from Form 10-K filings, ESG/CSR reports, and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s database. Methodology: How TIME and Statista Determined America's Top Manufacturers of 2027 Most of the companies fall in the Industrial & Electrical Equipment sector (64), followed by companies in Electronics & Semiconductors (48)—both sectors that Trump claims are growing in America due to tariffs. Biopharma also dominates, making up 70% of the top 10, with Eli Lilly leading the list, the first drugmaker to hit $1 trillion in market share, due to the demand for its weight-loss drugs. As part of a $27 billion investment, the company is building four new manufacturing facilities in the U.S., which it says will create 13,000 manufacturing and construction jobs. In a report that the White House published on Nov. 1, it declared “America is in the midst of a Manufacturing Renaissance,” boasting about $380 billion in investments towards manufacturing plants. But other industry experts aren’t seeing a renaissance. Economic policy analysts at the Center for American Progress reported earlier this year that since Trump announced tariffs in 2025, 89,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost—“the equivalent to the closure of more than 2,800 average-size manufacturing establishments nationwide.” They report that the war in Iran has made it harder to manufacture in America because it’s led to higher freight costs and supply chain shortages. Rachel Slade, author of Making It in America: The Almost Impossible Quest to Manufacture in the U.S.A. (And How It Got That Way) , also argues that it isn’t Trump, but his predecessor Joe Biden, who “put policies in place to incentivize investment in the Rust Belt and struggling economies, and we are starting to see the fruits of that.” One example she cites is the 2021 Build America, Buy America act , which mandated that federally-funded public infrastructure projects use American-made iron, steel, and construction materials. Other efforts designed to boost manufacturing include the Inflation Reduction Act and the CHIPS act (acronym for “Creating Helpful Incentives to Produce Semiconductors”), both enacted in 2022. Manufacturing abroad—known as offshoring—has always been a hot-button political issue, but especially after the North American Free Trade Agreement was negotiated under President George H.W. Bush’s administration. It received bipartisan support because, as Slade sums up the thinking back then, “It would be better for Americans if stuff was made cheaply. We could then buy more because stuff is cheaper, and companies could make more profit because they were manufacturing for less…and we don't have to deal with the stress of working with environmental laws, labor laws.” Slade argues that Trump’s tariffs paradoxically make it harder to manufacture in the U.S. because “if you are tariffing raw goods, parts that they need, their costs go way up, and then it just becomes so much more difficult to manufacture in America.” J. Christopher Love, faculty co-director of the MIT Initiative for New Manufacturing, says summing up the state of American manufacturing is complicated: “We have really strong manufacturing here in the United States, and that it's not uniformly declining or uniformly thriving. What we have is a lack of consistency across the entire industrial base.” He argues that economic policies should not only be about bringing manufacturing back to America but also bolstering the manufacturing capabilities already stateside, equipping them with the latest technologies. “We shouldn't be trying to rebuild a manufacturing economy from another era.” Case in point, as data center construction explodes amid an AI boom, the electrical equipment sector of manufacturing is surging—and that's the industry boasting the most companies on the TIME list of America’s top manufacturers. One of these manufacturers is Generac (no. 85) which Reuters reports is planning a $250 million factory expansion by the end of 2027 so it can make new versions of its generators for data centers. Analysts at Wood Mackenzie predict that the U.S. data center electrical equipment market will grow from $20 billion in 2025 to $65 billion by 2030, making up 40% of the total US electrical equipment market.
